concepts.name: DNA replication
concepts.description: Learners should understand that reproduction involves making a copy of DNA, which is not perfectly accurate and leads to variation.
concepts.evidence: The basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy.

concepts.name: Binary fission
concepts.description: Learners should know that unicellular organisms reproduce by splitting into two daughter cells.
concepts.evidence: Amoeba splits into two halves during cell division; this is binary fission.

concepts.name: Multiple fission
concepts.description: Learners should recognize that some parasites produce many daughter cells simultaneously.
concepts.evidence: The malarial parasite Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells at the same time; this is multiple fission.

concepts.name: Fragmentation
concepts.description: Learners should understand that multicellular filaments can break into pieces, each developing into a new individual.
concepts.evidence: In simple multicellular organisms such as Spirogyra, the filament breaks into smaller pieces, and each piece grows into a new individual.

concepts.name: Regeneration & budding
concepts.description: Learners should be able to differentiate regeneration (whole organism from a piece) from budding (outgrowth that detaches).
concepts.evidence: In budding, as in Hydra and yeast, a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one site; the bud develops into a tiny individual, and when fully mature, it detaches from the parent and becomes a new independent individual.

concepts.name: Vegetative propagation
concepts.description: Learners should know that many plants reproduce asexually from roots, stems, or leaves, producing genetically similar offspring.
concepts.evidence: In many plants, new plants develop from parts such as the root, stem and leaves.

concepts.name: Spore protection
concepts.description: Learners should understand that spores are enclosed in thick walls that safeguard them until favorable conditions arise.
concepts.evidence: Spores are covered by thick walls that protect them until they come into contact with a moist surface and can begin to grow.

concepts.name: Pistil anatomy
concepts.description: Learners should identify the three parts of the pistil: ovary, style, and stigma.
concepts.evidence: The pistil, in the centre of the flower, is the female reproductive part; it has three parts: the swollen bottom part is the ovary, the middle elongated part is the style, and the terminal sticky part is the stigma.

concepts.name: Pollination & fertilisation
concepts.description: Learners should distinguish self‑pollination from cross‑pollination and describe the pollen tube pathway leading to fertilisation.
concepts.evidence: The transfer of pollen grains from the stamen to the stigma is called pollination. If it happens within the same flower it is self-pollination; if pollen is transferred from one flower to another, it is cross-pollination.

concepts.name: Human puberty & reproduction
concepts.description: Learners should recognize the physiological changes at puberty and the basic structure of male and female reproductive systems.
concepts.evidence: The period of adolescence during which the reproductive tissues begin to mature is called puberty.

concepts.name: Menstruation cycle
concepts.description: Learners should know the monthly cycle of egg release, possible fertilisation, and shedding of the uterine lining if fertilisation does not occur.
concepts.evidence: If the egg is not fertilised, it lives for about one day; the thick, spongy lining of the uterus is then not needed and slowly breaks and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucus.

concepts.name: Reproductive health methods
concepts.description: Learners should identify various contraceptive and disease‑prevention methods, including barriers, hormonal, intra‑uterine, and surgical options.
concepts.evidence: Methods to avoid pregnancy include mechanical barriers such as condoms; hormonal methods such as oral pills, which change the hormonal balance of the body so that eggs are not released; devices such as the loop or the copper‑T placed in the uterus; and surgical methods, in which the vas deferens in males or the fallopian tube in females is blocked.
